title: Trump and Tech Giants Agree to 'Self-Police' AI
paragraphs: US President Donald Trump and leaders of some of the world's biggest technology companies have signed a voluntary agreement aimed at making artificial intelligence safer.

The deal was signed at a White House meeting on September 29 by Trump and executives from Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia and xAI. It comes amid growing public concern about the risks of the rapidly developing technology.

Under the agreement, companies pledged to monitor their AI systems for risks and have internal teams check that their safeguards are working. Independent outside reviewers would also assess those safeguards, while committees within each company's board of directors would oversee the process.

Trump described the agreement as "morally binding," but it is not legally enforceable. Although it leaves open the possibility of turning these measures into laws, it puts responsibility for managing AI risks in the hands of the companies themselves.
"They understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters.

He praised the executives for developing technology that he said would produce "unbelievable growth." Earlier that day, he also unveiled America.gov, an AI chatbot designed to help Americans navigate government services, and promised not to restrict AI's development.

However, even some industry leaders expressed caution. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has called for a slowdown in AI development, said the technology has "very real risks" and that how to address them remains under discussion.
Some experts questioned whether the agreement goes far enough. Several measures are things the companies already do or have previously promised to do.

Robin Jia, a computer scientist at the University of Southern California, warned against putting too much faith in self-policing. Pointing to recent AI-related hacking incidents, he said the consequences would grow as the technology improves.

Other critics said the agreement's language was too vague. Alex Pascal, executive director of the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, argued that reducing AI's risks requires strong laws and regulation, as well as reducing the competitive pressure that pushes AI companies to make unsafe decisions.
